strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and underexplored setting: sequential unlearning requests for text-to-image diffusion models. The formulation distinguishes successful erasure, preservation of earlier erasures, and retention of unrelated capabilities.

Provides a clear empirical diagnosis of utility collapse and compares sequential, simultaneous, and independent unlearning. The parameter-drift measurements offer a useful perspective on why straightforward sequential application of existing methods fails.

Evaluates several compatible mitigation strategies, including L1/L2 regularization, selective fine-tuning, model merging, and semantic gradient projection, with broadly consistent findings across ConAbl and EraseDiff and across style and object concepts.
The semantic-interference analysis is intuitive, and the proposed projection method appears complementary to generic regularizers, producing sizable improvements when combined with them.
weaknesses: The evaluation is too narrow to support the general claims: it uses one UNLEARNCANVAS-derived model, one benchmark, only style/object concepts, and apparently a single randomly sampled sequence of 12 requests. There are no results across multiple sequences, orderings, seeds, architectures, or standard pretrained checkpoints, and the plots provide no uncertainty estimates.

Unlearning and retention are measured almost exclusively through specialized classifier accuracy. This does not establish actual removal, robustness to paraphrases or adversarial prompts, preservation of image quality and diversity, or resistance to concept recovery. Human evaluation and perceptual/generative-quality metrics are absent.

The comparison set is limited. The paper does not adequately compare against adapted continual-learning approaches such as replay, EWC/SI, GEM/A-GEM-style constraints, or stronger recent concept-erasure and preservation methods, despite motivating its techniques from these literatures.

The theoretical justification is overstated. The displayed second-order Taylor expression uses the Hessian at the pretrained parameters as an equality without a remainder or quadratic-loss assumption. The resulting upper bound does not show that parameter distance determines retention, and the random-direction gradient-difference ratio is not an estimate or bound of the Hessian operator norm. Thus it does not validate the claimed causal explanation.

The gradient-projection method is underspecified. The manuscript omits essential details about LLM-generated auxiliary concepts, filtering thresholds, number of concepts, prompt/model choices, numerical treatment of the potentially singular Gram matrix, and the exact matrix-wise projection implementation. Sensitivity analyses for these choices and comparisons to using known retained concepts are also missing.

Reproducibility is weak overall: training hyperparameters, regularization strengths, selection/merging sparsities, computational costs, and per-method numerical results are largely absent. Several important conclusions must be inferred from small plots rather than tables or statistical tests.

The paper presents model merging as a continual remedy, but independently training and retaining a model for every request plus repeatedly merging all prior updates may have substantial time and storage costs. These costs are not quantified against sequential and simultaneous baselines.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and practically motivated setting: unlearning requests often arrive sequentially, whereas most diffusion-model unlearning work assumes a batch of simultaneous requests.

The distinction among unlearning accuracy, in-domain retention, and cross-domain retention is useful, and the experiments consistently expose severe retention collapse for both style and object sequences.

The study covers two established unlearning methods, ConAbl and EraseDiff, and evaluates several compatible mitigation strategies. The reported gains from gradient projection and its combinations are substantial.
The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and visually communicates the main empirical phenomenon effectively.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is too narrow for the paper's broad claims: it uses one fine-tuned Stable Diffusion checkpoint, one benchmark, apparently one sampled request order per setting, and only two base unlearning methods. There are no repeated permutations, uncertainty estimates, alternative diffusion architectures, or tests on realistic identities, copyrighted content, or harmful concepts.

Reproducibility is poor. Essential details for the proposed method are missing, including the auxiliary-concept LLM and prompt, the number of concepts, similarity model and filtering threshold, projection implementation, hyperparameter selection, and computational overhead. The promised cost comparison for simultaneous unlearning is not actually quantified.

The gradient-projection formulation is technically unclear and potentially incorrect. Gradients with respect to W_K and W_V are matrices, yet the derivation treats the gradient as a vector in the text-embedding space and applies (I-P_S)g. Preserving Wc would ordinarily require projecting along the matrices' input dimension, e.g. an appropriately oriented right projection. The scalar orthogonality lemma does not establish invariance of the attention keys, values, generated images, or retention loss.

The theoretical analysis provides little support for the central causal account. The displayed second-order Taylor expression omits a remainder term, the Hessian-at-the-initial-point bound is not justified for finite parameter changes, and a bound involving both linear and quadratic terms is inaccurately described as Lipschitz continuity. Correlation between parameter distance and retention does not show that drift is the cause of collapse.

Evaluation relies almost entirely on benchmark classifiers. Unlearning accuracy defined as failure to predict the target can reward generic image degradation, while no FID-like quality metric, prompt-alignment metric, human evaluation, adversarial recovery test, or privacy/copyright-oriented measure establishes genuine concept removal. A few qualitative examples do not close this gap.

The semantic analysis is based primarily on one target style ('Abstractionism') and simple correlations over only twelve concepts, without significance tests or replication across targets. Ablations for the auxiliary subspace—nearest versus random concepts, subspace size, embedding choice, and possible overlap with evaluation concepts—are absent.

Several claims are overstated: 'first systematic study,' 'prohibitive' simultaneous-unlearning cost, and a 'principled solution' are not supported by sufficiently broad comparisons or measurements. Relevant continual-learning baselines such as replay, EWC-style importance regularization, or established gradient-memory methods are discussed but not evaluated.

The paper lacks a meaningful limitations and risk discussion. Because ineffective unlearning can create false assurances of regulatory compliance or safety, robustness against paraphrases, alternate prompts, and concept recovery should be central rather than omitted. Overall, the problem and initial findings are worthwhile, but the technical ambiguity and incomplete evaluation leave the work below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper identifies a timely and practically important setting—sequential concept-unlearning requests for text-to-image diffusion models—and clearly demonstrates that standard unlearning methods can suffer severe retention collapse in this setting.

The empirical narrative is coherent: sequential updates accumulate substantially more parameter drift than simultaneous or independent unlearning, motivating regularization-based remedies that consistently improve retention.

The study covers style and object removal, two representative unlearning algorithms (ConAbl and EraseDiff), multiple generic regularizers, and combinations with the proposed gradient-projection method. Unlearning accuracy, in-domain retention, and cross-domain retention are tracked throughout the request sequence.

The semantic-interference analysis is insightful. The reported relationships among text-embedding similarity, changes to cross-attention keys/values, and retention degradation provide useful motivation for projecting updates away from nearby concepts.

Gradient projection produces strong in-domain retention and is complementary to selective fine-tuning and model merging. The resulting improvements are large, particularly after many sequential requests.
The presentation is clear and well organized, with informative figures, explicit definitions, and an appendix containing additional results and theoretical context.
weaknesses: The experimental scope is narrow for the paper's broad claims: all results use one UNLEARNCANVAS-fine-tuned Stable Diffusion checkpoint, one dataset, and apparently one randomly sampled sequence per setting. There are no repetitions over request orderings, uncertainty estimates, or tests on standard pretrained models and more realistic removal requests such as identities, copyrighted subjects, or unsafe content.

Evaluation relies almost entirely on benchmark-specific classifiers. Classifier evasion is not equivalent to genuine concept removal, and the paper provides no human evaluation, independent semantic metrics, image-quality metric, or adversarial/paraphrased prompting analysis to establish robust unlearning and perceptual preservation.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including the regularization coefficients and selection sparsities, the number and identities of auxiliary concepts, the LLM and prompt used to generate them, the similarity filter, and sensitivity analyses for these choices. The project-page entry is also blank in the submitted manuscript.

The theoretical component is limited. The Taylor bound is generic and does not establish that minimizing global parameter distance preserves generation accuracy; the assertion that the gradient and Hessian are small near the pretrained model is insufficiently justified, and the reported random-perturbation estimate of smoothness is only weak evidence for the relevant optimization trajectories.

The comparison set is modest. Only two base unlearning methods are tested, while stronger concept-preservation methods and more direct continual-learning baselines such as replay, Fisher-weighted regularization, or episodic gradient constraints are not empirically compared.

Efficiency is central to the motivation, but the paper reports no concrete wall-clock time, memory, storage, or cumulative-compute measurements. This is particularly important because model merging requires independently unlearning and retaining multiple models, while gradient projection additionally depends on external LLM-generated concepts.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and practically motivated setting—sequential unlearning requests for text-to-image models—and clearly separates continual, simultaneous, and independent unlearning protocols.

The empirical observation of utility collapse is compelling and appears consistently across ConAbl and SculpMem, with additional celebrity-erasure and SDXL/ESD experiments providing useful evidence beyond the primary UnlearnCanvas setting.

The proposed regularizers are modular and compatible with existing unlearning algorithms. The gradient-projection combinations yield large reported improvements; for example, the harmonic mean rises from 37.8 to 89.6 when combined with selective fine-tuning in style unlearning.

The distinction between in-domain and cross-domain retention is insightful. The correlation between semantic similarity, cross-attention distortion, and retention degradation motivates a useful direction for semantic-aware preservation.
The paper is generally well organized, provides helpful qualitative illustrations, studies training cost and parameter drift, and includes several complementary analyses in the appendix.
weaknesses: The main evaluation appears to use only one randomly sampled concept sequence per setting, with no repetitions, error bars, confidence intervals, or sensitivity to request order. Continual-learning results can be highly order-dependent, so this substantially weakens the empirical conclusions.

Reproducibility is poor: the manuscript does not specify learning rates, regularization coefficients, top-k values, optimization schedules, auxiliary-concept count, LLM and prompt used to generate auxiliaries, similarity threshold, text encoder, or tuning protocol. No executable code or complete experimental configuration is identified.

Unlearning accuracy is defined merely as classifier failure on templated prompts. This rewards image degradation and does not demonstrate genuine removal. The evaluation lacks stronger concept-recovery tests, prompt paraphrases, adversarial extraction, embedding-based leakage checks, and human assessment of targeted outputs.

The theoretical justification is overstated. The displayed second-order Taylor expression is treated as an equality with the Hessian fixed at the pretrained parameters without a remainder term, and the resulting norm bound is generic; it neither establishes causality nor shows that parameter drift is the dominant source of retention loss. The reported curvature trend has only four perturbation scales and a nonsignificant Spearman result (p=0.2).

The gradient-projection derivation is dimensionally underspecified: gradients of key/value projection matrices are matrices, whereas the method and lemma operate on a vector g. Preserving auxiliary embeddings requires a clearly defined right projection such as G(I-P), and the inverse in C(C^T C)^-1 may not exist without rank assumptions or a pseudoinverse.

The benchmark remains narrow despite the appendix extensions: the primary results use a benchmark-finetuned Stable Diffusion model, fixed prompt templates, small closed concept vocabularies, and at most 12 requests. This is distant from open-world deletion requests and does not establish long-horizon behavior.

Computational and storage tradeoffs are incompletely characterized. Model merging requires independently trained checkpoints, while gradient projection requires external LLM-generated concepts and projection computation; these costs are not compared systematically with baselines.

Overall, the problem and results are promising, but missing statistical validation, incomplete implementation details, weak unlearning verification, and overclaimed theoretical support place the paper slightly below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and practically motivated setting: concept-removal requests arriving sequentially rather than in a single batch. The demonstrated retention collapse is a useful observation for diffusion-model unlearning research.
The empirical scope is broader than a minimal proof of concept: experiments cover styles, objects, and celebrity identities; ConAbl, SculpMem, and ESD; and both the UnlearnCanvas model and SDXL.

The proposed regularizers are modular and generally maintain high reported unlearning accuracy while improving retention. Combining selective fine-tuning or model merging with gradient projection produces substantial gains in several settings.

Separating in-domain from cross-domain retention is informative. The observed relationship between semantic similarity and collateral degradation provides a plausible direction for more targeted preservation methods.

The manuscript is organized clearly, includes qualitative examples and computational-cost analysis, and openly frames its contribution as an empirical study with compatible add-ons rather than a complete native continual-unlearning algorithm.
weaknesses: The central theoretical argument is technically unsound as written. The second-order Taylor expansion is presented as an equality using the Hessian at the pretrained parameters but omits the remainder term; the resulting bound therefore does not hold generally. It also does not establish that parameter distance causes retention loss or that update norm is the dominant factor. The finite-difference experiment samples random directions rather than estimating the Hessian operator norm, reports weak statistics (e.g., Spearman p=0.2), and provides no meaningful scale against which the claimed 'minuscule' curvature can be judged.

The main evaluation appears to use only one randomly sampled request sequence and one held-out concept set, with no repetitions over request order, concept selection, training seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. Order sensitivity is fundamental in continual learning/unlearning, so single trajectories cannot support claims of robust or systematic superiority.

The primary metrics can conflate genuine concept removal with classifier evasion or degraded generation: UA counts any classifier mistake as successful unlearning. The main style/object benchmark lacks human evaluation, perceptual-quality metrics, alternative classifiers, paraphrased prompts, compositional prompts, and adversarial recovery tests. Consequently, the experiments demonstrate suppression under a narrow protocol rather than reliable machine unlearning, privacy removal, or irrecoverability.

The gradient-projection presentation is under-specified and dimensionally imprecise. Gradients of the key/value projection matrices are matrices, but the derivation treats them as embedding-space vectors; the necessary row-wise projection or right multiplication is not formally stated. First-order invariance applies only to the projected cross-attention update and does not guarantee preservation of generated concepts when other parameters, nonlinear layers, contextualized multi-token embeddings, and repeated optimization steps change.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Essential details such as regularization coefficients, pruning percentages, optimizer settings, anchor selection, auxiliary-concept count, LLM and prompt used to generate auxiliaries, similarity thresholds, hyperparameter-selection protocol, and sensitivity analyses are absent. No ablation establishes which auxiliary concepts or projection choices matter.

Baseline coverage is too limited for the paper's regularization perspective. It omits natural continual-learning and interference-control baselines such as replay/preservation losses, EWC-style importance regularization, GEM/A-GEM or orthogonal-gradient variants, and relevant concept-preserving gradient approaches. Comparing mostly against naive sequential application makes the gains difficult to contextualize.

Efficiency claims are incomplete. Model merging independently trains and stores a growing number of models, while auxiliary-concept generation and projection introduce additional costs; these compute, memory, and storage requirements are not reported. The L1/L2 penalties also constrain distance from the immediately preceding checkpoint rather than the pretrained model, which does not directly implement the paper's stated cumulative-drift objective.

Several conclusions are overstated relative to the evidence, including causal attribution of collapse to parameter drift, characterization of cross-attention projections as the key source of interference, and broad generalization to continual machine unlearning. Overall, the topic and empirical signal are promising, but the invalid theoretical support, fragile evaluation protocol, missing baselines, and poor reproducibility place the work below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically important and underexplored setting: text-to-image unlearning requests arriving sequentially. The formulation distinguishes erasure of new targets, preservation of earlier erasures, and retention of unrelated capabilities.

The central empirical finding—rapid utility collapse under sequential unlearning—is clear and consequential. Comparisons with independent and simultaneous unlearning, parameter-drift measurements, early-stopping controls, and training-cost analysis provide a coherent account of the phenomenon.

The proposed regularizers are modular and practically useful. In particular, semantic-aware gradient projection is well motivated by the observed relationship between embedding similarity and collateral degradation, improves in-domain retention, and combines effectively with selective fine-tuning or model merging.

The evaluation has encouraging breadth: it covers styles, objects, and celebrity identities; ConAbl, SculpMem, and ESD; and both Stable Diffusion and SDXL. Results consistently support the main empirical conclusions, and the paper evaluates both target removal and multiple dimensions of retained utility.

The manuscript is clearly organized, communicates its main insights effectively, and includes useful qualitative analyses of interpolation behavior, anchor-dependent updates, and the efficiency gap between sequential and simultaneous approaches.
weaknesses: The continual benchmark appears to use only one sampled ordering of target concepts in each principal setting, with no variation across request orders, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. Since continual-learning outcomes can be highly order-dependent, evidence across several independently sampled sequences is important.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the proposed methods and benchmark. Essential details such as regularization coefficients, sparsity ratios, learning rates, complete stopping rules, auxiliary-concept generation prompts, the number of auxiliary concepts, similarity thresholds, and sensitivity analyses are missing or difficult to recover; no usable code or project link is provided in the manuscript.

The theoretical argument is weaker than presented. The second-order Taylor expression omits an explicit remainder or intermediate-point Hessian, and the resulting norm bound is a generic local upper bound rather than evidence that parameter drift causes retention loss. The finite-difference directional curvature proxy does not estimate an operator-norm bound and is not directly connected quantitatively to retention accuracy.

The semantic-interference motivation is demonstrated primarily through one target style, “Abstractionism.” Establishing the claimed general relationship requires aggregating correlations across many targets and separating semantic similarity from classifier difficulty or other concept-specific confounders.

Classifier error is a limited measure of successful unlearning: it may reflect altered image quality or classifier evasion rather than removal of the target representation. The study lacks adversarial recovery tests, stronger membership or reconstruction analyses, and human evaluation of whether concepts are genuinely erased while image quality is preserved.

The baseline coverage remains somewhat narrow. More direct adaptations of continual-learning mechanisms such as EWC, GEM/A-GEM, replay, or orthogonal-gradient methods would better establish whether the proposed projection and regularization choices outperform established anti-forgetting strategies rather than selected generic baselines. Model merging also has nontrivial storage and per-request training costs whose scaling is not fully analyzed.
